name: Sleeping on your back

lead: Some looksmaxxers sleep on their backs so the face stays off the pillow, aiming to avoid sleep lines, the creases that form when the face is pressed into a pillow or mattress for hours.

The idea is that avoiding repeated overnight compression of facial skin reduces creasing over time. Wikipedia's article on wrinkles states that habitual sleeping positions are linked to wrinkles, citing a dermatology-society resource, but gives no study detail. No published trial has tested whether changing sleep position alters facial wrinkles.

paras: People train themselves to sleep face-up, often using a supportive pillow arrangement so they stay on their back. Lateral (side) sleeping is the most common adult position, followed by supine, then prone.
Sleep research links supine sleep to worse positional sleep apnea, reflux after meals and more sleep paralysis in some people. It is not discussed as a cosmetic risk.

angle.text: Some looksmaxxing practitioners sleep face-up to avoid sleep lines caused by pressing the face into a pillow for hours. With the face off the pillow there is no overnight compression, so fewer creases form. Habitual sleep position is linked to wrinkles in reference sources, and no trial has tested changing position.

lead: Sleeping on your back (the supine position) is a sleep habit that some looksmaxxers adopt to keep the face from being pressed into a pillow for hours each night. The aim is to avoid so-called sleep lines, the creases on the forehead, cheeks and around the eyes that practitioners attribute to side or stomach sleeping, and so keep the skin looking smoother and more symmetrical over time.[1][2][3]

Dermatology literature does describe sleep wrinkles as a distinct category. A 2016 review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal by Anson, Kane and Lambros separated sleep wrinkles from expression wrinkles and proposed that compression, shear and stress on the face in lateral or prone sleep may create them.[3] A 2026 study in Anais Brasileiros de Dermatologia examined frontal wrinkles in older adults and the association of sleep lines with sleep quality.[3] Wikipedia's wrinkle article lists habitual sleeping position among the factors linked to wrinkling, citing an American Academy of Dermatology resource.[2]

Adults sleep in three main positions: lateral, supine and prone, with lateral the most common.[1] Back sleeping is also the position most associated with positional obstructive sleep apnea, so sleep medicine treats it as a trade-off outside of appearance.[1][4]

paras: The practice consists of lying face up for sleep rather than on the side or stomach, so that the face is not compressed against a pillow or mattress. Some adherents combine it with pillow choice or other overnight habits; the details vary by person.
Sleep-position references describe lateral sleeping as most common in adults, followed by supine and then prone, and report that lateral preference rises with age and body mass index.[1]

The 2016 Aesthetic Surgery Journal review titled "Sleep Wrinkles: Facial Aging and Facial Distortion During Sleep" distinguishes sleep wrinkles from expression wrinkles, which differ in cause, location and pattern. It proposes that compression, shear and stress from lateral or prone positions may create wrinkles and may also contribute to expansion of facial skin.[3]

Wikipedia's wrinkle article lists habitual sleeping position alongside glycation, loss of body mass and sun damage as processes linked to wrinkles, and cites the American Academy of Dermatology's aging-skin resource for the statement.[2] It also describes a misrepair-accumulation theory in which repeated stretching and compression of skin injures elastic and collagen fibres, which are replaced by altered fibres, leading to folds.[2]
A 2026 paper in Anais Brasileiros de Dermatologia by Campos and colleagues reports on prevalence and patterns of frontal wrinkles in elderly people and on how sleep lines relate to sleep quality.[3]

Sleep-medicine reviews describe supine position as the most common phenotype of positional obstructive sleep apnea, in which airway collapse is more frequent when lying on the back than on the side.[4] Wikipedia reports that positional apnea accounts for roughly 56 to 75 percent of regular obstructive sleep apnea cases, and that lying supine soon after eating is linked to laryngopharyngeal reflux and supine sleep to sleep paralysis.[1]
People with these conditions are generally treated with positional therapy that moves them off the back, which makes the position a consideration beyond appearance.[4]

The sleep-wrinkle literature is primarily descriptive. The 2016 Anson, Kane and Lambros review proposes mechanisms by which side and stomach sleeping may create wrinkles, and the 2026 Campos study looks at sleep lines in older adults.[3][3] No published trial was found that randomises people to back sleeping and measures wrinkle change.
Studies of supine sleep itself are mainly in sleep medicine, covering positional sleep apnea and its treatment.[4]

timeline.event: Anson, Kane and Lambros publish a review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal separating sleep wrinkles from expression wrinkles.[3]
A Sleep Medicine Reviews article reviews the classification, epidemiology and treatment of supine-related obstructive sleep apnea.[4]
Campos and colleagues publish a study of frontal wrinkles and sleep lines in older adults in Anais Brasileiros de Dermatologia.[3]
